words.definition: the process of converting information into a code to prevent unauthorized access
words.example: End-to-end encryption ensures that only the sender and recipient can read a message's contents.

words.definition: close and continuous observation of a person or group, especially by an authority
words.example: Mass surveillance programs collect vast quantities of data on ordinary citizens who are never suspected of wrongdoing.

words.definition: conducted with secrecy, typically because it is illicit or officially disapproved of
words.example: The agency's clandestine data-collection operation was exposed only after a leaked internal memo surfaced.

words.definition: present, appearing, or found everywhere
words.example: Facial-recognition cameras have become almost ubiquitous in major metropolitan centers.

words.definition: to act so as to limit or undermine a right or entitlement
words.example: Civil liberties groups argue that indiscriminate data collection infringes upon the right to privacy.

words.definition: the state of being unidentified or unnamed
words.example: Encrypted messaging apps grant users a degree of anonymity that traditional communication channels cannot.

words.definition: a gap created in security defenses that allows unauthorized access, or an act of violating a law or agreement
words.example: The data breach exposed the personal records of nearly two hundred million users.

words.definition: a systematic and comprehensive search or surveillance operation that captures large amounts of information indiscriminately
words.example: Privacy advocates decry dragnet surveillance for treating every citizen as a potential suspect.

words.definition: a weakness in a system that can be exploited to compromise its security
words.example: The researchers disclosed the software vulnerability to the company before publishing their findings.

words.definition: to take advantage of a weakness or flaw for one's own benefit, especially unethically
words.example: Hackers exploited an unpatched vulnerability to infiltrate the ministry's servers.

words.definition: not openly acknowledged or displayed; secret
words.example: The covert monitoring of activists' phone records triggered a parliamentary inquiry.

words.definition: a person who exposes secret information or activity within an organization that is deemed illegal or unethical
words.example: The whistleblower's disclosures prompted a global reckoning over the scope of state surveillance.

words.definition: a discouraging or inhibiting effect on legitimate behavior, especially free speech, caused by fear of consequences
words.example: Pervasive monitoring can produce a chilling effect, deterring citizens from expressing dissenting political views.

words.definition: not transparent or clear; difficult to understand or account for
words.example: The algorithm governing the watchlist remains opaque even to the officials who administer it.

words.definition: the state of being answerable for one's actions, especially to a higher authority or the public
words.example: Without judicial oversight, intelligence agencies operate with little meaningful accountability.

words.definition: appropriate or corresponding in size, degree, or amount relative to the aim being pursued
words.example: Courts must weigh whether a surveillance measure is proportionate to the threat it purports to address.

words.definition: to intrude gradually and often stealthily on someone's territory, rights, or freedoms
words.example: Critics fear that expanded biometric tracking will steadily encroach on the private sphere.

words.definition: a hypothetical system of surveillance in which all occupants can be observed at all times, used metaphorically for pervasive monitoring
words.example: Scholars describe the modern smart city as a digital panopticon in which residents are perpetually watched.

words.definition: a defensive structure or safeguard; a person or thing that protects against harm
words.example: Independent courts serve as a bulwark against executive overreach in matters of state surveillance.

words.definition: the state of being involved with others in an illegal or unethical activity
words.example: Journalists accused several telecommunications firms of complicity in the government's covert data-sharing scheme.

text: The expansion of state surveillance capacity poses a dilemma that resists easy resolution. Governments justify ubiquitous monitoring — from dragnet data collection to covert wiretapping — as an indispensable bulwark against terrorism and organized crime. Yet the same infrastructure that promises security can just as readily infringe on the anonymity that underwrites free expression. When citizens suspect that dissent is being logged, a chilling effect follows: people self-censor not because they have broken any law, but because the machinery of observation is so pervasive, and its criteria for suspicion so opaque, that caution becomes the only rational response. Proponents insist that such measures remain proportionate, narrowly tailored to genuine threats; critics counter that once a clandestine surveillance apparatus is built, its scope tends to encroach steadily beyond its original mandate, exploiting every legal ambiguity and technical vulnerability along the way. The 2013 disclosures by a former intelligence contractor, still the most consequential whistleblower episode of the digital era, revealed a system whose accountability mechanisms had scarcely kept pace with its capabilities. Technology firms, too, face accusations of complicity, having quietly enabled access to user data. The question, ultimately, is not whether security and liberty can coexist, but who decides where the boundary lies.

questions.question: What is the central tension the author identifies in the passage?
options: Between economic growth and environmental protection
Between the security benefits of surveillance and its threat to civil liberties
Between domestic and international law
Between whistleblowers and journalists

questions.question: According to the passage, why does a 'chilling effect' occur even among law-abiding citizens?
options: Because laws explicitly criminalize dissent
Because uncertainty about opaque surveillance criteria leads people to self-censor out of caution
Because citizens are unaware that surveillance exists
Because whistleblowers encourage people to stop speaking

questions.question: The author's reference to the 2013 disclosures serves primarily to:
options: Illustrate a historical example where oversight failed to match surveillance capability
Prove that all surveillance is illegal
Discredit the intelligence contractor personally
Suggest that whistleblowing is always ethically justified

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the relationship between surveillance infrastructure and its original mandate?
options: Surveillance systems typically remain confined to their initial, narrow purpose
Surveillance systems tend to expand beyond their original scope over time
Surveillance mandates are always reduced after public criticism
There is no relationship between infrastructure and mandate

questions.question: What is the author's tone toward technology firms accused of enabling data access?
options: Enthusiastically supportive
Implicitly critical, framing their role as a form of complicity
Completely neutral and uninterested
Openly congratulatory

questions.question: How does the passage's concluding question function rhetorically?
options: It resolves the debate definitively in favor of security
It reframes the debate away from an either/or choice toward a question of authority and decision-making
It dismisses the entire discussion as irrelevant
It suggests that liberty and security can never coexist under any circumstances
